newsitem.title: USA: Whitewater's Starr hints Clinton probe not over.
newsitem.headline: Whitewater's Starr hints Clinton probe not over.

text.p: Whitewater prosecutor Kenneth Starr said on Monday he planned to step aside to become dean of a California university law school, but hinted that the probe into President Bill Clinton's finances would continue.

Starr said he had accepted the post of law school dean at Pepperdine University in Malibu, California, and would leave the politically charged Whitewater investigation to start his new job by August 1.
The announcement immediately led to speculation that Starr had decided not to seek indictments against the president and first lady Hillary Rodham Clinton or senior White House aides.
But Starr cautioned reporters not to jump to conclusions.
"I would read nothing into this except that it is an extraordinary professional opportunity for me," Starr said after flying into Little Rock from Washington late on Monday.
He said the probe into the Clintons' personal and business finances was "active and ongoing" and hinted that it would continue beyond his own resignation.

"We have many able and competent professionals both in Little Rock and Washington who are very familiar with the investigation. The office will be, I am sure, in very good hands," Starr said, adding that much could happen between now and August.
Starr, 50, has led the independent Whitewater investigation since August 1994 and his decision to step aside comes at a crucial time in the complex probe.
According to press reports, Starr's staff has in recent weeks been weighing the pros and cons of bringing criminal charges against the Clintons, White House aides and other government officials.
The Clinton administration declined to comment Monday on Starr's planned resignation, but privately one Clinton aide said: "There are a lot of smiles around the White House."
The investigation has cast a long shadow over Clinton's presidency and the president's allies have accused Starr of having a Republican bias.
Some of Starr's critics said Monday they thought he might be stepping down because he has failed to find any firm evidence against the Clintons.

"I think the investigation is petering out," said David Williams, the attorney for Patsy Thomasson, a White House aide and longtime friend of the Clintons. Thomasson came under Starr's scrutiny as part of his probe into the suicide of deputy White House counsel Vincent Foster and the "Travelgate" firings at the White House travel office.
Williams said Starr's team has become more quiet in recent months. "Last summer they were hot and heavy but we haven't heard a peep from them since August last year."

The investigation at first focused on a failed real estate venture in Arkansas in which the Clintons were passive investors but it has since grown to include their personal finances and those of business associates and political allies.

Starr won a major victory in May last year when a Little Rock jury found businessman James McDougal and his ex-wife Susan -- partners of the Clintons in the Whitewater real estate development -- guilty on a string of fraud charges.
Arkansas Gov. Jim Guy Tucker, who was not involved in the Whitewater land deal, was also found guilty of two charges.
Clinton testified on behalf of the defence in that trial, and James McDougal is now cooperating with Starr's team but no charges have yet been filed against the president or his wife.

Starr appeared to be closing in on the White House after winning the convictions against the McDougals but suffered a setback last August when two bankers who were political allies of Clinton were acquitted of fraud and conspiracy charges.

When asked who would replace him, Starr said that would be decided by the three-judge panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia which named him to replace original Whitewater independent counsel Robert Fiske in 1994.
